19.01.title: Capstone method
19.01.html:
Phase 19 is ten capstone projects in the style of an ETH Fokus-Projekt or Bachelor thesis. Each one pulls several phases together: a fluid solver and a field measurement, a FEM model and a safety factor, a controller and a thermal limit. Before the first one, this lesson sets out the method that turns “I worked on a turbine” into “here is the evidence that it meets its requirements”.

Requirements you can test

A good requirement is specific, measurable and verifiable: “deliver at least 2.0 kW electrical at the design flow”, not “be efficient”. Write each one with an ID, a number and a unit. Then decide how it will be verified:

  • Test: measure it on the built thing.
  • Analysis: compute it with a model you have validated.
  • Inspection: look at it, for example check a weld or a drawing.
  • Demonstration: show it working, for example a fresh clone that rebuilds every figure.

The verification matrix

The verification matrix is a table with one row per requirement and the tests that close it. Two rules make it useful: every requirement has at least one test, and every test traces to a requirement. A requirement without a test is a hope. A test without a requirement is effort that proves nothing anyone asked for. The matrix in the code below fails loudly if either rule breaks, so it can run in continuous integration next to the analysis code.

The critical path

List the tasks with their durations and predecessors. A forward pass gives each task’s earliest start ES=max(EFpred​) and earliest finish EF=ES+d. A backward pass from the end date gives the latest finish LF=min(LSsucc​) and latest start LS=LF−d. The float LS−ES is how far a task can slip without delaying the project. Tasks with zero float form the critical path: any slip on them moves the hand-over date week for week.

Risk

For each risk, score the likelihood L and the impact I on a 1 to 5 scale. The product L×I ranks them. Mitigate the top ones first, and write down the score you expect after mitigation, so that you can check later whether it worked.

Worked examplePlan a micro-hydro capstone

A 2 kW turbine for a village in Bali (lesson 19.05 sizes it).

  1. Requirements. R1: at least 2.0 kW electrical. R2: runner stress below half of yield at runaway speed. R3: the penstock survives the water hammer of a 2 s valve closure. R4: frequency within 50 ± 1 Hz from 20 % to 100 % load. R5: all figures rebuild from a fresh clone in under 10 minutes.
  2. Matrix. Six tests close the five requirements. R1 is closed twice, by a test (2.31 kW) and an analysis (2.42 kW). The code asserts that every requirement has a passing test and every test has a requirement. The measured values here are illustrative: in your project they come from your own lessons and measurements.
  3. Schedule. Nine tasks. The forward and backward passes give 16 weeks. The critical path is A-B-C-E-G-H-I; the penstock design (D) and the pipe and generator purchase (F) have 2 weeks of float each.
  4. Risk. The top risk is a dry-season flow below the design flow (4×4=16). Sizing for the flow exceeded 90 % of the time and measuring in August brings it to 8. The runner casting (12), village interest (10) and a late generator (9) follow.

Exercise 1Find the critical path

Tasks: P (3 weeks), Q (2 weeks, after P), R (4 weeks, after P), S (1 week, after Q and R). How long is the project, which tasks are critical, and how much float does Q have?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Forward pass: P 0 to 3, Q 3 to 5, R 3 to 7, S starts at max(5,7)=7 and ends at 8. The project takes 8 weeks.
  2. Backward pass: S has LS 7, so R has LF 7 and LS 3, and Q has LF 7 and LS 5.
  3. Critical path P-R-S. Q has 5−3=2 weeks of float.

quiz.q: Earliest finish (weeks) of a 3-week task whose predecessors finish at weeks 4 and 6.
quiz.explain: ES = max(EF of predecessors) = 6, EF = 9.

quiz.q: Float (weeks) of a task with ES = 5 and LS = 8.
quiz.explain: LS − ES.

quiz.q: Risk score for likelihood 3 and impact 5.
quiz.explain: L × I.

quiz.q: A requirement with no test in the verification matrix:
quiz.explain: Every requirement needs evidence.
options: Should be removed from the matrix
Is fine if the design is good
Is unverified, so the project cannot claim it

quiz.q: A one-week slip on a task with two weeks of float:
quiz.explain: It stays within the float, though the task now has only one week left.
options: Delays the project by one week
Makes the task critical with negative float

19.02.title: "Coconut eddy: from field video to CFD"
19.02.html:
Lesson 17.10 asked why a coconut can circle behind a boulder in a Bali river for minutes on end. This capstone closes the loop the way a real study would: measure the coconut’s path from video, model the eddy, and compare the two, explaining whatever does not agree. The scene itself is in the Coconut lab.

The pipeline

  1. Film from a fixed point above the river, with two markers a known distance apart in the frame for the scale (and four for a full perspective correction).
  2. Background. The median of many frames over time is the river without the coconut.
  3. Detect. Subtract the background, blur a little (single bright pixels from sun glints disappear), threshold, and take the intensity-weighted centroid of what remains.
  4. Track. Predict the next position with constant velocity and only search a window around it. If the coconut is lost, search the whole frame again.
  5. Convert pixels to metres and frames to seconds, then compute what the model can predict: the orbit period around the eddy centre and the residence time, the time until the coconut leaves a box 4D long behind the boulder.

The model

The kinematic wake of lesson 17.10: uniform flow U past a cylinder of radius a, with Föppl’s pair of vortices on the curve r−a2/r=2y and their images. The strength that holds the pair stationary is

Γ=4πUy0​(1−r04​a4​).

Real eddies have a finite core, so the point vortex is smoothed with a factor d2/(d2+rc2​) at distance d from the centre. Shedding is modelled by wobbling the two strengths in antiphase at the Strouhal frequency, Γ(1±εsinωt) with ω=2πStU/D.

What to expect

In the steady model the streamlines inside the bubble are closed, so the coconut never leaves. With shedding, fluid crosses the bubble edge in lobes once per cycle and the motion becomes chaotic: two coconuts released 3 cm apart can leave a minute or ten minutes apart. A single measured residence time is therefore one sample from a wide distribution. The fair comparison is: does the measurement fall inside the model’s spread?

Worked exampleTrack it and compare

Honest note: no field footage was available to the machine that built this course, so the “video” is synthetic: 240 s at 10 frames per second and 2 cm per pixel, rendered from the unsteady model with ε=0.22, rc​=0.25 m, a 1 m boulder and U=0.4 m/s, plus water texture, noise and sun glints. The tracking code does not know any of this and would run unchanged on real frames.

  1. Föppl pair. At x0​=1.2 m the curve gives y0​=0.5702 m and Γ=2.809 m²/s. With point vortices the induced velocity at the vortex is zero to 10−3, so the formula holds.
  2. Tracking. The coconut is found in 1822 frames, and it drops fewer than 3 % of frames before it leaves. The median position error is 0.29 cm, under a fifth of a pixel. The worst is 7.3 cm, when the blob overlaps glints.
  3. Measured. The coconut circles the eddy 80.6 times with a mean orbit period of 2.30 s and leaves the 4D box after 185.7 s.
  4. Steady model from the measured release point: orbit period 2.11 s, 8.6 % shorter than measured, and 40 neighbouring release points are all still trapped after 240 s. The steady model gets the circling right and the escape completely wrong.
  5. Unsteady model, 60 release points within the 3 cm tracking uncertainty: 58 % escape within 240 s, and the residence times have 10 %, 50 % and 90 % points of 28.8 s, 154.0 s and more than 240 s. The measured 185.7 s lies inside that range.
  6. Discrepancy explained. The escape comes from the shedding, not from the mean eddy. The orbit period differs because the wobble enlarges the orbits. On a real river, wind on the coconut and its own inertia add further differences, and ε has to come from the CFD of lesson 17.09 or from the eddy’s own wobble in the video.

Exercise 1Plan the field day

You will film from a bridge 6 m above the water with a phone at 30 frames per second and 1920 pixels across a 12 m wide view. The coconut moves at up to 1 m/s. How many pixels is a 15 cm coconut, how far does it move between frames, and how should you size the search window?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Scale: 12/1920=6.25 mm per pixel, so the coconut spans 24 pixels.
  2. At 1 m/s and 30 fps it moves 33 mm per frame, about 5.3 pixels.
  3. A window of about 3 times the frame-to-frame motion plus the coconut’s radius, roughly 30 pixels, keeps it even when the velocity prediction is off. Fix the phone on a tripod, because camera shake moves everything.

quiz.q: Shedding frequency (Hz) behind a 1.5 m boulder in a 0.6 m/s river, St = 0.2. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: f=StU/D.

quiz.q: Föppl strength Γ (m²/s) for U = 1 m/s, a = 1 m, y₀ = 1 m, r₀ = 2 m. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: 4πUy0​(1−a4/r04​).

quiz.q: Scale (mm per pixel) for a 10 m wide view across 2000 pixels. 1 decimal.
A steady recirculation bubble traps a tracer for ever because:
quiz.explain: In steady flow, particle paths are streamlines.

quiz.q: The fair way to compare one measured residence time with a chaotic model is:
quiz.explain: Chaotic advection makes single trajectories unpredictable.
options: Check that it falls inside the model’s spread from nearby release points
Require the model to match it exactly

19.03.title: "Subak weir network: water balance for terraced fields"
19.03.html:
Bali’s subak system has shared river water between rice terraces for about a thousand years. A weir in the river feeds a canal, proportional dividers split the canal between groups of farmers, and the water then steps down from field to field over small outlet weirs. This capstone models a small network for a year and asks the question every farmer asks in August: does the water reach my field? You can explore the real system in the Subak lab.

Weirs

A sharp-crested rectangular weir of width b with head H above the crest passes

Q=32​Cd​b2g​H3/2,

with Cd​≈0.62. A proportional divider puts several notches at the same crest level. They all see the same head, so each passes a flow in proportion to its width, whatever the total:

∑k​Qk​Qi​​=∑k​bk​bi​​.

That is why the subak cuts the notch widths in proportion to each group’s land: the share stays fair in a flood and in a drought.

Water balance of one terrace

Each field of area A holds a ponding depth h. Over a time step Δt,

AΔh=(Qin​−Qout​)Δt+PAΔt−VET​−Vperc​,

where Qout​ is the outlet weir flow with head h−hc​ above the crest hc​, P is rain, and evapotranspiration and percolation take about 5 mm and 3 mm a day. The outflow of one terrace is the inflow of the next one down.

The update is written so that every cubic metre is booked exactly once. Each loss is capped at what the field actually holds, so the depth can never go negative. The test is then strict: the ledger must close at every terrace to rounding error, and the whole network must close as well.

Worked exampleA year on a 1.9 ha network

Three branches of four terraces with 8400, 6600 and 4200 m² of rice. The outlet crests are 5 cm high and 30 cm wide. The river flow, rain and season are assumed, not measured: 60 to 80 L/s in the wet season (November to April) with afternoon showers, and 3 L/s in the dry season. The intake takes half the river, up to 25 L/s.

  1. Divider. Notches of 200, 157.1 and 100 mm. At 6 cm head they pass 5.382, 4.228 and 2.691 L/s, shares of 0.4375, 0.3438 and 0.2188, exactly the land shares.
  2. Mass balance. The worst terrace balance error over the year is about 10−13 of the water that passed through it. The network takes in 438 871 m³ of canal water and rain, and the outflow to the river, the losses and the change in storage add up to the same number.
  3. Dry-season demand. 8 mm/day×19200 m2 is 1.778 L/s, and the intake delivers 1.5 L/s, 84 % of the demand.
  4. Proportional split. The top three terraces of every branch keep standing water all dry season. The tail-end terraces have it only 33 to 35 % of the time, because each field fills to its crest before it passes anything on.
  5. Rotation. Sending the whole flow to one branch for 5 days at a time spreads the shortage: the worst terrace is still near 35 %, but branch 3’s tail-end field rises from 33 % to 65 %. The mean over all fields falls from 0.836 to 0.660, because fields that dry out between turns lose water to re-wetting.

So rotation is fairer to the tail, at a cost in total. In practice the subak’s water temple schedule also staggers planting so that not every field needs full water at once, which this model does not include.

Exercise 1Fill a field

A dry 2000 m² terrace with a 5 cm outlet crest receives 5 L/s from the canal while losing 8 mm a day. How long does it take before water starts to spill to the next field? And once full, how long would it stay wet if the canal stopped?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Volume to the crest: 2000×0.05=100 m³.
  2. Losses: 0.008×2000/86400=1.85×10−4 m³/s, so the net inflow is 4.815×10−3 m³/s.
  3. Time to fill: 100/4.815×10−3=20770 s, about 5.77 h.
  4. With no inflow the 5 cm lasts 50/8=6.25 days, which is why a 5-day rotation keeps most fields wet.

quiz.q: Flow (m³/s) over a 0.3 m wide sharp-crested weir with 0.1 m head, Cd = 0.62. 5 decimals.
quiz.explain: Q=32​Cd​b2g​H3/2.

quiz.q: A divider serves 8400, 6600 and 4200 m². The first notch is 200 mm. Width (mm) of the second? 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Widths in proportion to land.

quiz.q: Dry-season demand (L/s) of 19 200 m² of rice losing 8 mm a day. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Depth per day times area, divided by 86 400 s.

quiz.q: A proportional divider keeps the share fair at any flow because:
quiz.explain: Same head, so Q is proportional to b.
options: The water speed is the same everywhere
All notches share one crest level and see the same head
The notches are the same width

quiz.q: In a shortage, rotating the whole flow between branches:
quiz.explain: Fields that dry between turns lose water to re-wetting.
options: Helps tail-end fields but lowers the network’s average wetted time
Makes every field wet all the time

19.04.title: "Bamboo footbridge: FEM, statics and the joints"
19.04.html:
A 6 m footbridge over an irrigation canal, built from local bamboo. This capstone sizes it with the direct stiffness method of Phase 10, checks the result two independent ways, and then finds what actually governs. Try breaking a truss first in the Break the bridge lab.

Not a design. The strengths, bolt capacities and safety factors below are assumptions for teaching. Bamboo varies a lot between species, culms and seasons, and it rots and splits. A bridge people walk on needs tested material, a recognised code (for example ISO 22156 for bamboo structures) and a licensed engineer.

The structure

Two Pratt trusses 1 m deep, six 1 m panels, with the deck hung from the bottom chords. Every member is a culm of 80 mm outside diameter and 8 mm wall, so

A=4π​(D2−d2)=1809.6 mm2,I=64π​(D4−d4)=1.187×106 mm4.

With 12 nodes, 21 members and 3 support reactions, m+r=2j: the truss is statically determinate, so the forces do not depend on E and can be checked by hand.

Loads and checks

  • Loads per truss: a crowd of 4 kPa and a deck of 0.6 kPa on a 1.2 m deck, factored by 1.5 and 1.35, so w=4.086 kN/m.
  • Members: axial stress against assumed characteristic strengths of 40 MPa in compression and 80 MPa in tension, divided by 2.
  • Buckling: pin-ended Euler, Pcr​=π2EI/L2, also divided by 2.
  • Joints: a 12 mm bolt through a mortar-filled node, assumed good for 4 kN.
  • Deflection: crowd only, unfactored, against L/250.

Statics gives an independent check at midspan, Nchord​=wL2/(8H). Virtual work, δ=∑Ni​ni​Li​/(EA) with ni​ the forces from a unit load, checks the FEM displacement.

Worked exampleSize the bridge

  1. FEM. The reactions are 12.26 kN at each end, which carries the 24.52 kN total load. The top chord across midspan carries −18.387 kN and the bottom chord +16.344 kN.
  2. Statics. wL2/(8H)=4.086×36/8=18.387 kN, equal to the top chord force to machine precision. A section through the bottom chord panel next to midspan gives 16.344 kN, also exact.
  3. Virtual work. The midspan deflection under the factored load is 7.185 mm by both methods. Under the crowd alone it is 4.22 mm, far inside L/250=24 mm.
  4. Members. The worst member is the top chord at 0.51 utilisation in compression. Buckling of a 1 m panel is only 0.21, and of the 1.41 m end post 0.33.
  5. Joints. With one bolt at each member end, the joint carrying the top chord would be at 4.60, overloaded more than four times. The joints govern by far.
  6. Redesign. Run the chords as continuous culms through the nodes, so a node only carries the web members. The diagonals then need 1 to 3 bolts and the end posts 4, and every check passes.

The lesson from real bamboo structures is the same: the culm is strong, the connection is the problem.

Exercise 1The end post

The end post runs at 45° from the support to the first top node. The support reaction is 12.26 kN and the load at the end node is 2.043 kN. Find the end post force, its stress and its buckling utilisation with a factor of 2, using E=15 GPa.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Vertical equilibrium at the support node: the post carries 12.26−2.043=10.215 kN vertically, so N=10.2152​=14.446 kN in compression.
  2. Stress: 14446/1809.6=7.98 MPa, against 40/2=20 MPa, a utilisation of 0.40.
  3. Buckling: Pcr​=π2×15×109×1.187×10−6/2=87.9 kN for the 1.414 m post. Divided by 2 that is 43.9 kN, so the utilisation is 0.33.

quiz.q: Area (mm²) of a bamboo culm, 100 mm outside diameter, 10 mm wall. 5 significant figures.
quiz.explain: 4π​(D2−d2).

quiz.q: Midspan chord force (kN) for w = 3 kN/m, L = 8 m, H = 1.2 m. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: wL2/(8H).

quiz.q: Euler load (kN), pin-ended, E = 15 GPa, I = 1.187e-6 m⁴, L = 2 m. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: π2EI/L2.

quiz.q: A plane truss with 12 nodes, 21 members and 3 reactions is:
quiz.explain: m+r=24=2j.

quiz.q: In bamboo trusses, what usually governs?
quiz.explain: Bamboo splits at bolts long before the culm fails.
